中西功.note: 1910–1973. A Japanese Communist and China expert who worked for the South Manchuria Railway’s research arm while spying for the CCP under Pan Hannian’s system; obtained strategic intelligence on Japan’s southern advance. Arrested by the Tokkō, tried, and freed at the war’s end; later a Japanese Communist Party member of the Diet.

尾崎秀实.note: 1901–1944. Asahi Shimbun journalist, China expert, and adviser to Prime Minister Konoe, and the key Japanese member of the Sorge ring; arrested in 1941 and hanged with Sorge in 1944. Not to be confused with Ozaki Shōtarō.

尾崎庄太郎.note: A left-leaning graduate of the East Asia Common Culture Academy and member of Nakanishi Kō’s network; a different man from the Sorge-ring spy Ozaki Hotsumi.

王学文.note: 1895–1985. A Japan-trained Marxist economist and secret Communist who taught at the Japanese academy in Shanghai and later directed the Eighth Route Army’s enemy-army work and the Japanese Workers’ and Peasants’ School at Yan’an.

郑文道.note: 1914–1942. Nakanishi Kō’s Chinese liaison; arrested by the Japanese gendarmerie in 1942, he took his own life to protect the network.

西里龙夫.note: A Japanese journalist and Common Culture Academy man who joined the Communist intelligence network in Nanjing; tried with Nakanishi Kō and freed in 1945.

今井武夫.note: 1898–1982. A Japanese army officer who ran Operation Kiri, the secret 1940 peace channel to Chongqing, and later negotiated the Japanese surrender in China.

东条英机.note: 1884–1948. The Japanese army general who became prime minister in October 1941 and led Japan into the Pacific War; executed as a war criminal in 1948.

吴成方.note: A Communist intelligence officer under Pan Hannian who ran the Japanese cell in Shanghai; imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case and rehabilitated in 1982.

汪锦元.note: A secret Communist planted as a secretary at Wang Jingwei’s side, feeding the regime’s top secrets to the Pan Hannian network.

川合贞吉.note: A Japanese member of the Sorge ring, introduced to Sorge by Agnes Smedley.

池步洲.note: 1908–2003. A Japan-trained Nationalist cryptanalyst who broke Japanese diplomatic ciphers; Chinese accounts credit him with forecasting a Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, a claim not independently corroborated abroad.

荒尾精.note: 1859–1896. A Japanese army officer and pioneer of Japanese intelligence work in China, who opened the Hankou branch of the Rakuzendō pharmacy as a cover.

根津一.note: 1860–1927. A Japanese army officer and educator who founded and long directed the East Asia Common Culture Academy in Shanghai.

高崇武.note: So printed in the source; the man is the documented Gao Zongwu (高宗武), who with Tao Xisheng exposed the draft Japan–Wang Jingwei treaty in the January 1940 “Gao-Tao incident.”

宋子良.note: The name the “Nationalist” negotiator used in Operation Kiri. Song Ziliang was a real member of the Soong family (a brother of T.V. Soong and Soong Mei-ling), but the man at the negotiating table was an impostor, an agent of Dai Li’s Juntong.

满铁.note: The South Manchuria Railway Company, a vast Japanese “state-policy company” that ran the railways and much of the economy of the Northeast and doubled as a huge intelligence organ; its Research Department was a magnet for spies. Abbreviated 满铁 (Mantetsu).

关东军.note: The Japanese army in the Northeast, grown from the SMR’s railway guards into the driving force of Japanese aggression in Manchuria and the chief force facing the Soviet Union.

东亚同文书院.en: the East Asia Common Culture Academy
东亚同文书院.note: The Tōa Dōbun Shoin, a Japanese academy in Shanghai (founded 1901) that trained Japanese “China hands” and doubled as a nursery of intelligence officers; a Communist Party branch also grew up inside it.

东亚同文会.en: the East Asia Common Culture Society
东亚同文会.note: The Tōa Dōbunkai, the semi-official Japanese society that founded and oversaw the academy.

太平洋调查会.note: The IPR, an American-founded international academic body that met by turns around the Pacific rim, and whose views could sway the relevant governments.

兴亚院.note: The Asia Development Board, a Japanese cabinet organ set up in 1938 to run affairs in occupied China, with a special-service department that drew the secret services under one hand.

关特演.note: The Kantokuen (関特演), a huge July 1941 mobilization of the Kwantung Army against the Soviet Union after the German invasion; never carried out, as Japan chose the southern advance.

桐工作.note: The Kiri Kōsaku (桒工作), Japan’s most secret 1940 “peace” channel to Chongqing, run by Imai Takeo; 桒 is the paulownia (kiri).

拉穆塞小组.note: Sorge’s Tokyo intelligence cell, from his radio code name “Ramsay”; the source also transliterates it 拉姓扎.

李得森.note: A Chinese member of Nakanishi Kō’s Nanjing network, arrested by the Japanese in 1942.

钱明.note: Real name Jing Ruonan; a Chinese liaison of the Nakanishi Kō cell and Zheng Wendao’s schoolmate.

刘钊.note: Pan Hannian’s secret courier in the Jiangnan area and Zheng Wendao’s Party sponsor.

张明达.note: A courier of the Nakanishi Kō cell who escaped the 1942 arrests; later wrote about the network under the name Fang Zhida (方知达).

ch06.anchor: opened in Yan'an a Japanese Workers' and Peasants' School
ch06.note: A real institution (日本工农学校), opened at Yan’an on 15 May 1941 to re-educate Japanese prisoners of war; it was led by the Japanese Communist leader Nosaka Sanzō (who used the alias Okano Susumu, 冯野进). Its graduates carried out antiwar propaganda at the front. CORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: the memorial that the Japanese prime minister Tanaka Giichi had submitted to the Emperor, which said: "To conquer the world, one must first conquer China
ch06.note: The so-called Tanaka Memorial. Its authenticity is rejected by most Japanese and Western historians: no Japanese original has ever surfaced, and it is generally regarded as a fabrication that appeared in China around 1929. Its expansionist program did, however, foreshadow the actual course of Japanese aggression, which is why it was so widely believed. The circulation described here is itself well attested: Yan Baohang obtained a copy and had an English translation distributed to Western delegates at the 1929 IPR conference in Kyoto. CONTRADICTED as a genuine state document; the author reports it, as the Chinese side of the day received it, as authentic.

ch06.anchor: A Survey of China's War-Fighting Strength
ch06.note: The Japanese-language report used the exonym Shina (支那) for China, as in Shina Expeditionary Army and the “China Incident” below; once a neutral term, it had become a slur by this period. It is rendered plainly as “China” throughout.

ch06.anchor: the most highly classified of all the peace operations, "Operation Kiri
ch06.note: Operation Kiri (the Kiri Kōsaku) was a genuine 1940 Japanese channel to Chongqing run by Imai Takeo. The negotiator called “Song Ziliang” used the name of a real Soong brother, but the man at the table was an impostor, an agent of Dai Li’s Juntong; mainstream accounts treat the affair as a Nationalist deception that strung the Japanese along. Pan Hannian did run an intelligence-exchange tie to Iwai Eiichi and did expose the impostor to him. The book’s dramatized version—that Pan cast the man as a Communist plant so the Japanese would fear a Juntong trap—and the credit it gives Pan for collapsing the channel rest on Chinese accounts. PARTLY CORROBORATED.

So printed in the source. The man is the well-documented Gao Zongwu (高宗武), who with Tao Xisheng defected from the Wang Jingwei camp to Hong Kong and published the draft treaty in January 1940—the “Gao-Tao incident.” The source’s 崩 for 宗 is a misprint.

ch06.anchor: the plan for the "Kwantung Army Special Maneuvers,"
ch06.note: The Kantokuen (関特演) of July 1941 was a real and enormous mobilization—on the order of 700,000 to 800,000 troops—massing the Kwantung Army in the Northeast for a possible strike at the Soviet Union after the German invasion. Japan ultimately shelved it and turned south. CORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: moved the 200,000-strong army defending the eastern front against Japan to the western front, and won at last the defense of Moscow
ch06.note: The Soviet transfer of Far Eastern divisions west in the autumn of 1941 is real and mattered to the defense of Moscow, though modern scholarship qualifies the “Siberian divisions saved Moscow” picture: only some units were genuinely Siberian, and some moves preceded any decisive intelligence. The reporting usually credited for freeing these forces is Sorge’s (and Soviet code-breaking), not Chinese Communist intelligence. The book’s attribution of the decision specifically to the Communists is a Chinese account and is UNCORROBORATED; see the note in Chapter 5 on the Barbarossa warning.

ch06.anchor: On December 7, 1941, Japan will launch surprise attacks at many points across the Pacific
ch06.note: That the Nakanishi–Ozaki network reported Japan would go south, meaning war with the United States and Britain, is well attested; the precise prediction of the Pearl Harbor date recorded here rests on later Chinese accounts (chiefly Nakanishi’s own) and is not independently corroborated. PARTLY CORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: Chi Buzhou broke another special cipher telegram
ch06.note: Chinese accounts credit the Nationalist cryptanalyst Chi Buzhou with reading Japanese diplomatic traffic and forecasting a Sunday attack on Pearl Harbor, a warning said to have been passed to and ignored by the Americans. The story is widely repeated in China but is not corroborated in Western records of the Pearl Harbor intelligence. UNCORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: so that people call him "the Yue Fei of Japan."
ch06.note: Yue Fei (1103–1142) was a Southern Song general celebrated as the archetype of the loyal soldier who dies for his country; to call the ancestral General Kusunoki Masashige “the Yue Fei of Japan” casts him in the same mold of martyred loyalty.

ch06.anchor: like Zhuge Liang pacifying the Five Routes from the calm of his own home
ch06.note: An allusion to the Romance of the Three Kingdoms: the strategist Zhuge Liang, without stirring from his residence, turns back five invading armies at once by arranging countermeasures in advance—a byword for commanding great events from a quiet center. Zhuge Liang is the same strategist of the Empty City Stratagem (Chapter 5).

ch06.anchor: The greatest sound is silent; the greatest form has no shape.
ch06.note: From Laozi’s Daodejing, chapter 41: the received text reads the greatest sound is faint of voice (大音希声); the source prints 大音无声. The saying is turned here into an emblem of the spy who works unseen and unheard.
